name: Ravioli
look: Flat square pillow of two pasta sheets with a crimped, fluted border.
fact: Recorded in Italy since the 14th century. The crimped edges are as much about sealing in the filling as decoration.

name: Raviolini
look: Miniature square ravioli, about a thumbnail across.
fact: Small enough to eat by the spoonful, they are most often cooked and served in broth rather than sauced.

name: Ravioloni
look: Oversized square ravioli, three or four to a plate.
fact: The extra size leaves room for chunky or delicate fillings such as mushrooms, seafood or whole pieces of cheese.

name: Agnolotti
look: Small square parcel of thin egg pasta, cut with a fluted wheel.
fact: In Piedmont, leftover roast meat traditionally became the filling, and the roasting juices became the sauce.

name: Agnolotti del plin
look: Tiny rectangular parcel with a pinched pleat between each mound of filling.
fact: "Plin" means "pinch" in Piedmontese: each tiny parcel is sealed with a pinch of the fingers. Filled with roast meats, they are sometimes served plain in a folded napkin.

name: Tortelli d'erbetta
look: Slim rectangular parcel with fluted edges, green filling showing through the thin dough.
fact: Parma's chard-and-ricotta tortelli are the traditional dish of the night of San Giovanni, 23 June, eaten outdoors swimming in melted butter and Parmigiano.

name: Tortelli di zucca
look: Plump square or rectangular parcel with an orange filling.
fact: Mantua's Christmas Eve dish: the filling mixes pumpkin with crushed amaretti and mostarda (mustard-spiced fruit) for a sweet-sharp flavour dating to Renaissance court cooking.

name: Tortelli maremmani
look: Very large square ravioli, generously stuffed and cut with a fluted wheel.
fact: From the Maremma of southern Tuscany, these outsized tortelli are filled with ricotta and spinach or chard and usually buried under a hearty meat ragù.

name: Tortelli di patate
look: Square ravioli with a soft, pale potato filling.
fact: A speciality of the Mugello and Casentino valleys of Tuscany: the filling is mashed potato seasoned with garlic, parsley and cheese, a thrifty mountain answer to meat fillings.

name: Spoja lorda
look: Tiny, flat fluted squares with only a thin smear of cheese inside.
fact: From Romagna: the sheet is merely "dirtied" with a thin layer of soft cheese, folded, and run over with a fluted wheel into tiny squares for broth.

name: Ofelle
look: Soft square or half-moon ravioli made from a potato dough.
fact: A Trieste speciality whose wrapper is a gnocchi-like potato dough, filled with spinach, veal and sausage.

name: Uovo in raviolo
look: One very large round raviolo with a whole raw egg yolk nested in a ring of ricotta and spinach.
fact: Created in 1974 at Ristorante San Domenico in Imola: cooked just long enough that the yolk runs when the raviolo is cut. Classically finished with butter and white truffle.
pairings: brown butter, Parmigiano and white truffle

name: Lune
look: Round disc-shaped ravioli with a crimped rim.
fact: Stamped out with a round cutter rather than cut with a wheel; the circular shape wastes more dough than squares but seals evenly all round.

name: Girasoli
look: Large round ravioli with a wide, deeply fluted border like petals.
fact: The broad scalloped rim around a domed centre gives the sunflower look; it is a modern shape, common in fresh-pasta shops.

name: Mezzelune
look: Semicircle made by folding a disc of pasta over its filling.
fact: Folding a disc in half needs only one sealed edge, making it one of the simplest and oldest ways to enclose a filling.

name: Schlutzkrapfen
look: Thin, darkish half-moon with a pressed edge and a green filling.
fact: From South Tyrol, where Italian and Austrian traditions meet: the dough includes rye flour and the filling is spinach and curd cheese or ricotta.

name: Casunziei
look: Half-moon with a pink blush where the beet filling shows through.
fact: The Ladin ravioli of Cortina d'Ampezzo and the Dolomites. The classic "red" version is filled with beetroot and dressed with melted butter and poppy seeds.

name: Casoncelli
look: Half-moon folded back on itself with a dent pressed in the middle.
fact: The Bergamo version stuffs them with meat, breadcrumbs, amaretti, raisins and pear, a sweet-savoury mix; Brescia makes its own, simpler style.

name: Cjarsons
look: Plump half-moon with a pinched or crimped edge.
fact: From the Carnia mountains. Fillings mix herbs, potato, raisins, cinnamon, even cocoa, recalling the cramârs, local peddlers who traded spices across the Alps.

name: Tordelli lucchesi
look: Large half-moon with a fork-pressed edge.
fact: "Tordello" is simply Lucca's way of saying tortello. Unusually, they are meat inside and out: a meat, chard and thyme filling under more meat ragù.

name: Ravioli capresi
look: Soft round ravioli with a domed centre.
fact: Capri's ravioli use an eggless dough made with boiling water and a filling of caciotta cheese, Parmigiano and marjoram.

name: Marubini
look: Small round (sometimes square or half-moon) ravioli with a fluted edge.
fact: Cremona's festive pasta, traditionally served "ai tre brodi", in a broth made from three meats: beef, chicken and pork.

name: Anolini
look: Small, smooth-edged discs about the size of a coin, slightly domed.
fact: The Christmas pasta of Parma and Piacenza. The Parma filling contains no meat itself, only the rich juices of a long-braised stracotto worked into breadcrumbs and Parmigiano.

name: Tortelli cremaschi
look: Half-moon whose edge is pinched into a row of little crests.
fact: The filling from Crema is famously sweet, with no meat or vegetables: amaretti, raisins, candied citron, grana and a spiced biscuit called mostaccino.

name: Gnocchi ripieni
look: Round potato dumpling, larger than a normal gnocco, hiding a filling.
fact: Potato dough wrapped around cheese, ham or mushrooms. The best-known traditional kind is the plum-filled gnocchi di susine of Trieste and Gorizia, served with buttered breadcrumbs.

name: Tortellini
look: Tiny ring made by folding a small square into a triangle and joining the corners round a fingertip.
fact: Legend says the shape was inspired by Venus's navel. Bologna and Modena both claim it; the pork, prosciutto and mortadella filling was officially registered in Bologna in 1974.

name: Tortelloni
look: Same folded ring as tortellini but several times larger and plumper.
fact: Larger than tortellini and usually filled with soft, meatless fillings such as ricotta and parsley, so it is sauced rather than served in broth.

name: Cappelletti
look: Small folded ring with a turned-up brim, like a tiny peaked hat.
fact: The name means little hats, and the folded brim is easy to spot. In Romagna the classic filling is cheese only; they are a Christmas dish served in capon broth.

name: Cappellacci
look: Large, plump folded hat with joined corners.
fact: Ferrara's larger, more rustic cousin of cappelletti, filled with violina pumpkin, Parmigiano and nutmeg. A pumpkin tortello was already recorded at the Este court in 1584.

name: Agnoli
look: Small folded ring much like a cappelletto, with a meat filling.
fact: Mantua's broth pasta. Tradition opens the meal with "sorbir d'agnoli": a few agnoli in a cup of hot broth with a splash of Lambrusco.

name: Balanzoni
look: Large green tortelloni made with spinach dough.
fact: Named after Dottor Balanzone, Bologna's pompous carnival character. The spinach dough encloses ricotta and mortadella.

name: Pansotti
look: Fat triangle (sometimes folded into a ring) with a bulging middle.
fact: These Ligurian parcels are meatless: filled with the wild herb mix called preboggion and cheese, and dressed with walnut sauce, not tomato or ragù.

name: Triangoli
look: Flat triangle made by folding a square corner to corner.
fact: The triangle is the half-way stage of a tortellino: stop after the first fold and you have a triangolo.

name: Culurgiones
look: Plump teardrop sealed along the top with a pleated seam like an ear of wheat.
fact: From Ogliastra in Sardinia, filled with potato, pecorino and mint. The hand-pleated seam, "sa spighitta", imitates an ear of wheat; they hold protected IGP status.

name: Tortelli piacentini
look: Slender plaited parcel tapering to a twisted tail at each end.
fact: Known in dialect as tortelli "with the tail". The ricotta and spinach filling is plaited into the dough; local legend says they were created in 1351 for a visit by Petrarch.

name: Caramelle
look: Filled rectangle twisted at both ends like a wrapped sweet.
fact: A strip of dough is rolled round the filling and the ends twisted or pinched. The shape is associated with festive tables in Emilia, around Parma and Piacenza.

name: Scarpinocc
look: Small parcel with two flared ends and a dent pressed in the centre.
fact: From the village of Parre near Bergamo, named for the cloth shoes once worn there. The filling is meatless: cheese, breadcrumbs and spices.

name: Fagottini
look: Square of pasta with its four corners brought up and pinched together over the filling.
fact: The four seams meet in a cross on top, so the bundle sits upright on the plate.

name: Sacchettini
look: Tiny drawstring purse with a ruffled, gathered top.
fact: The top is pinched into a tiny purse shape after filling. A popular modern filling is cheese with pear.

name: Cannelloni
look: Wide smooth tube about 10 cm long, wrapped round a filling.
fact: Traditionally a sheet of fresh pasta rolled around the filling rather than a pre-formed tube; they are filled first and baked second, under sauce and béchamel.

name: Manicotti
look: Very large ridged dried tube, stuffed and baked.
fact: The Italian-American cousin of cannelloni, stuffed with ricotta and baked in tomato sauce. Many Italian-American families make them with thin crepes instead of pasta.

name: Conchiglioni ripieni
look: Giant ridged conch shell with its hollow packed with filling.
fact: The shell is big enough to hold a spoonful of filling; they are par-boiled, stuffed, set open-side up in a dish and baked.

name: Lumaconi ripieni
look: Giant ridged snail-shell tube, pinched nearly shut at one end, filled and baked.
fact: One end of the big "snail" is almost closed, so it cups the filling and stops it running out in the oven.

name: Rotolo ripieno
look: A whole sheet rolled up like a Swiss roll around its filling, then cut into spiral slices.
fact: The filled sheet is rolled, wrapped tightly in a cloth and poached whole, then sliced and often browned in the oven with butter and cheese.

name: Pierogi
look: Plump half-moon with a pinched or crimped edge.
fact: Poland's national dumpling, boiled and often then pan-fried. The famous potato-and-curd-cheese "ruskie" are named for Ruthenia, not Russia.

name: Uszka
look: Tiny folded ring, like a miniature tortellino.
fact: Filled with wild mushrooms and floated in clear beetroot barszcz for the Polish Christmas Eve supper.

name: Kołduny
look: Small, juicy half-moon or round dumpling.
fact: Shared by Lithuania, Poland and Belarus and often credited to the region's Tatars. The filling is raw minced beef or mutton with marjoram, so it cooks into its own broth.

name: Varenyky
look: Half-moon with a pinched, often rope-twisted edge.
fact: Ukraine's boiled dumplings come savoury (potato, cabbage, curd cheese) or sweet, most famously with sour cherries. They are also eaten in Russia and across Eastern Europe.

name: Pelmeni
look: Small round dumpling of thin dough with the two ends joined, like an ear.
fact: The name comes from the Komi and Udmurt for "ear bread". Associated with Siberia and the Urals, where they were made in bulk and kept frozen outdoors through winter.

name: Khinkali
look: Large pouch twisted shut into many pleats with a thick topknot.
fact: Georgian soup dumplings: the raw spiced meat releases broth inside. You hold one by its doughy knob, bite, sip the juice, and leave the knob on the plate.

name: Mantı
look: Tiny pinched square pouch of dough, often no bigger than a chickpea.
fact: Found from Turkey across Central Asia, where they are larger and steamed. The tiny version of Kayseri is the Turkish classic, served under garlic yogurt and chili butter.

name: Kreplach
look: Small triangle of egg dough, sometimes with two corners joined.
fact: The dumpling of Ashkenazi Jewish cooking across Central and Eastern Europe, not of one country. Meat-filled, it is eaten in chicken soup before Yom Kippur and at Purim.

name: Maultaschen
look: Large flat rectangular pocket, around 8 cm long.
fact: Swabia's oversized ravioli of meat, spinach and bread. Legend says monks at Maulbronn hid meat inside pasta during Lent so that God would not see it.

name: Idrijski žlikrofi
look: Small hat-shaped dumpling with a dent pressed in the top.
fact: From the mining town of Idrija: filled with potato, onion, cured pork fat and herbs. In 2010 they became Slovenia's first EU-protected traditional speciality.

name: Kärntner Kasnudeln
look: Large round-bellied half-moon with a rope-like crimped edge.
fact: Filled with curd cheese, potato and a local mint. The decorative crimping is called "krendeln", and Carinthian lore held that a girl who could not krendel was not ready to marry.

name: Ravioles du Dauphiné
look: Very small, thin squares sold joined together in perforated sheets.
fact: Tiny French ravioli from around Romans-sur-Isère, filled with Comté, fresh cheese and parsley. They cook in about a minute and carry a protected geographical indication.

name: Sorrentinos
look: Large round ravioli with a high domed centre and a flat rim.
fact: An Argentine invention despite the Italian name, generally traced to Italian-immigrant restaurateurs in Mar del Plata. The classic filling is ham and cheese.

name: Jiaozi
look: Crescent with a pleated seam along its curved top.
fact: Northern China's everyday dumpling, boiled, steamed or pan-fried as potstickers. Families fold them together at Lunar New Year; the shape recalls old silver ingots, a symbol of wealth.

name: Wonton
look: Small bundle of very thin square wrapper scrunched or folded round a nub of filling.
fact: The Cantonese name is written with characters meaning "swallowing clouds". The wrapper is thinner than a jiaozi's and trails silkily in soup.

name: Xiaolongbao
look: Round, thin-skinned pouch gathered at the top into a swirl of fine pleats.
fact: From the Shanghai area, linked to the town of Nanxiang. Jellied stock is mixed into the pork filling and melts when steamed, which is how the soup gets inside.

name: Shumai
look: Open-topped cylinder with the wrapper gathered round the filling like a cup.
fact: Never sealed: the filling shows at the top. The Cantonese dim sum version is pork and shrimp in a thin yellow wrapper, often dotted with roe or carrot.

name: Har gow
look: Small translucent bonnet with fine pleats, pink shrimp showing through.
fact: A Cantonese dim sum benchmark. The see-through skin is made from wheat starch and tapioca starch rather than flour, and chefs are judged on the number of neat pleats.

name: Gyoza
look: Slim crescent pleated on one side, usually browned flat on the bottom.
fact: Japan's take on Chinese jiaozi, which spread widely after the Second World War. The skins are thinner, the filling more garlicky, and pan-frying is the norm.
pairings: soy, rice vinegar and chili oil

name: Mandu
look: Half-moon, often with its two ends joined into a round bonnet.
fact: Korean dumplings, steamed, boiled or fried. Fillings often include tofu, glass noodles and kimchi, and they go into rice-cake soup for Lunar New Year.

name: Momo
look: Round pleated pouch or pleated crescent, steamed.
fact: Tibetan in origin and now the favourite street food of Nepal, also eaten in Bhutan and northern India. Nepali momos come with a spicy tomato and sesame chutney.

name: Buuz
look: Round steamed pouch pleated to a small opening at the top.
fact: Mongolian mutton dumplings; the name is related to Chinese baozi. Families make them by the hundreds for Tsagaan Sar, the lunar new year.

name: Chuchvara
look: Very small folded square with joined corners, like a tiny tortellino.
fact: A family of tiny meat dumplings found from Central Asia to the Caucasus under related names. They are boiled and served in their broth; in Azerbaijan several should fit on one spoon.

name: Shish barak
look: Small lamb-filled ring shaped like a little hat.
fact: A Levantine dish of Lebanon, Syria and Palestine: the dumplings are simmered in a hot yogurt sauce. The name is related to Central Asian joshpara.
pairings: cooked yogurt sauce with mint and garlic

name: Aushak
look: Thin-skinned half-moon or square, boiled.
fact: Afghan dumplings filled with gandana, a local leek-like green (chives or scallions elsewhere), then topped with garlic yogurt, a meat or lentil sauce and dried mint.

name: Gürzə
look: Elongated dumpling closed with a plaited seam along the top.
fact: An Azerbaijani lamb dumpling, a winter dish, sealed with a braided pattern and served with yogurt and garlic.

name: Cepelinai
look: Big oval potato dumpling, pointed at both ends like an airship.
fact: Lithuania's national dish, made from grated raw and cooked potato round a meat or curd filling. Once called didžkukuliai, they were renamed after Zeppelin airships.

name: Kroppkakor
look: Round potato dumpling about the size of a small fist.
fact: Swedish potato dumplings filled with salt pork and onion, associated with Öland, Småland and Gotland. The mix of raw and boiled potato varies from island to mainland.

name: Bánh bột lọc
look: Small, chewy, translucent dumpling with shrimp visible inside.
fact: From Huế in central Vietnam. The wrapper is tapioca starch, turning glass-clear when cooked; the dumplings are boiled bare or steamed wrapped in banana leaf.
